children.value: The archivist of the radio station wants to mark where the talk ends and the music begins. Two recordings show the task: a man reading a novel aloud and a string orchestra playing a dance by Brahms. A listener needs a fraction of a second to tell them apart. A spectrogram, the energy of each frequency in each short frame, contains this information, but it is a large matrix: 40 ms frames with a hop of 20 ms turn the 14.8-second reading into 741 spectra of 442 bins each. A classifier and an index need a few numbers per frame and per segment that describe how the sound is heard.
Listeners describe sounds by a handful of perceptual attributes:

, the color of a sound that distinguishes a violin from a voice at the same pitch and loudness. Two more attributes describe mixtures: the texture of many overlapping sources, such as a busy market, and their location in space.

measure properties of the signal that correspond to these attributes. They come in three groups: features computed directly from the samples of a frame (time domain), features computed from its spectrum (frequency domain), and features that model the frequency resolution and loudness perception of the ear. A single frame of 40 ms says little about whether someone is speaking. The pattern over several seconds does: speech alternates between syllables and short pauses, about four to five syllables per second, while music tends to keep a more continuous level. Speech has many low-energy frames in its pauses and many high-ZCR frames in its hissing consonants, so both ratios tend to be higher for speech than for music.
The two running clips are the 14.8-second LibriVox reading of
and the 45.8-second Brahms recording by a string orchestra.

children.value: Frame zero-crossing rates (left) and LSTER and HZCRR per 4-second segment (middle, right) of the LibriVox reading and the Brahms clip.

The frame ZCR points the other way: Brahms crosses zero twice as often on average, because the strings produce many high harmonics. Most frames of the reading, its vowels and voiced consonants, cross zero rarely, and a long tail of hissing consonants reaches beyond 0.3. Speech does not cross zero more often on average; it varies more from frame to frame, and the ratios capture exactly this variation.

The 11 segments of the reading lie in narrow bands, because the rhythm of syllables and pauses stays the same throughout the reading. The Brahms segments spread widely. Ten of them reach at least the lowest LSTER of the reading (0.42), and all ten lie in the last 15 seconds, where the music changes its dynamics abruptly: a rest of the orchestra around 34 seconds, strong accents, and the fade-out from 42 seconds on. Like the pauses of speech, these contrasts put many frames below half the mean energy. Only three Brahms segments reach the lowest HZCRR of the reading (0.17), and only two, starting at 37 and 41 seconds, look like speech on both ratios. The highest HZCRR, 0.31, belongs to the last segment: in the fade-out, little more than noise remains, and its frames form the small bump near 0.55 in the left panel.

SB is the spread of the spectrum around its centroid: a pure tone has a small bandwidth, noise a large one. The
SF compares the normalized spectrum with that of the previous frame and is high when the sound changes abruptly, for example at the start of a note or a syllable. The

Energy measures what reaches the microphone, not what the listener hears.

(left) shows the equal-loudness contours: each curve connects the sound pressure levels at which pure tones of different frequencies sound equally loud to an average listener. The curves dip between 2 and 5 kHz, where the ear canal resonates and the ear is most sensitive, the range that also matters most for understanding speech. Near the threshold of hearing, a 50 Hz tone needs about 40 dB more than a 1000 Hz tone to sound equally loud, and at the level of a conversation still about 30 dB more.

children.alt: Equal-loudness contours (left) and the A, B, C, and D frequency weightings (right).

children.value: Equal-loudness contours (left) and the A, B, C, and D frequency weightings (right).
Frequency weightings approximate these contours with a correction

children.html: A(f)A(f)A(f)

children.value: in decibels that is added to the energy of each frequency before summing (

, right). The A-weighting of the international standard IEC 61672 is by far the most common, although it follows the contour of quiet sounds. It subtracts 30.3 dB at 50 Hz, 19.1 dB at 100 Hz, and 3.2 dB at 500 Hz, leaves 1000 Hz unchanged, adds 1.3 dB at 2500 Hz and 1.0 dB at 4000 Hz, and subtracts 2.5 dB at 10 kHz. Noise limits and the “dB(A)” values of sound-level meters use this weighting.

children.value: . This follows the logarithmic perception of loudness, and it has a second effect. A voice is a source, the vibrating vocal cords, filtered by the vocal tract, whose shape changes with each vowel and consonant. In the spectrum, the filter multiplies the source; after the logarithm, it adds to it. A change in recording level or microphone becomes a constant offset as well.
Apply a discrete cosine transform (DCT) to the 26 log energies and keep the first 13 coefficients:

children.value: the tilt from low to high frequencies, and the higher coefficients increasingly fine ripples. Keeping 13 coefficients keeps the smooth envelope, which reflects the vocal tract and the timbre, and drops the fine structure, which reflects the pitch.

The result is called a cepstrum, a play on the word “spectrum”, because it is in a sense the spectrum of a spectrum. The DCT has a further benefit: neighboring mel bands are strongly correlated, and the cosine coefficients are nearly uncorrelated, which suited the classifiers of the time with their diagonal covariance matrices.

The coefficients describe a frame in isolation. Their changes over time carry information about transitions between sounds, so the feature vector is extended with the first and second differences over neighboring frames:

children.value: varies more in speech than in music, because each new vowel and consonant reshapes the spectral envelope while an orchestra holds its timbre for longer. Computed with 26 bands between 300 and 8000 Hz, its standard deviation over all frames is 10.75 for the LibriVox reading and 7.26 for the Brahms clip. Four more public recordings confirm the pattern: two further LibriVox readings by other readers reach 12.84 and 10.50, while Tchaikovsky’s Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy and the jazz piece Vibe Ace reach 9.99 and 7.76. All three readings lie between 10.5 and 12.8, all three music pieces between 7.3 and 10.0. Like LSTER and HZCRR, this segment statistic is a classic feature for speech/music classification.
